name: Environment Reset and Bootstrap Users
objective: A full local environment reset; a tested two-step start that creates five default users with a permanent password; the writer workload moved to srv-default-writer; Airflow Bundles owned by this repository; README start and reset documentation.
scope: Included: reset script and command, bootstrap users and on-demand enforcement, role-platform-admin across Polaris/RustFS/Airflow/Jenkins and (by later request) Keycloak lakehouse realm-admin and JupyterHub admin, writer migration from write-service-account to srv-default-writer via lakehouse-writer, Bundles moved into infra-v2 with LAKEHOUSE_PROJECT_ROOT removed, one-time removal of ../opensource-lakehouse/.runtime, README. Excluded: deferred tpch-loader and starrocks, Airflow developer-role drift, Jenkins job as code, extensions (security, PBT, resiliency) off.
workstreams: Bootstrap users, platform-admin group, and enforcement
README, tests, Build and Test, and Deploy handoff

verification.details: See construction/build-and-test/build-and-test-summary.md. Live reset (16 containers, 7 volumes, 6 networks, 3 directories) and rebuild from nothing passed; product bootstrap and Spark smoke tables (prod, UAT, dev); five user logins with correct groups, permanent passwords, and Polaris roles; bootstrap-users.sh re-enforcement after drift with an unlisted user untouched; RustFS OIDC 7/7 and STS; Polaris negative cases; role matrix; Airflow start with Bundles in infra-v2 and broker token as srv-default-writer; platform-admin lakehouse realm admin (200) and master denied (403); JupyterHub login confirmed by the user. Jenkins verifier 8/9: the CI job is absent after the reset, an expected effect recorded as a follow-up. Contract tests 185 passed, 1 skipped, 2 pre-existing Airflow drift failures. Not run: verify-keycloak-outage.py.

major_requirements: scripts/lakehouse.sh reset deletes all lakehouse-local containers, data volumes, Jupyter homes, networks, and three generated .runtime directories, with a typed confirmation, --yes, and --dry-run.

Five bootstrap users (joe-developer, peter-analyst, maria-owner, srv-default-writer, platform-admin) with the permanent password ChangeM3!, created only when missing at start and reset to defaults by scripts/bootstrap-users.sh.
role-platform-admin is owner-equivalent in Polaris, RustFS, Airflow, and Jenkins; by later user request also lakehouse realm-admin in Keycloak and JupyterHub admin.
Airflow and Spark write as srv-default-writer through the lakehouse-writer client; Airflow Bundles live in this repository; README documents start and reset.
design_decisions: Reset selects resources by Compose project label, runtime-role label, exact volume and network names, and the lakehouse-jupyter-home- prefix; a path guard limits file deletion to three .runtime directories.
A single file, infra/keycloak/bootstrap-users.json, is the source for users, groups, and the default password; start never changes existing users.
platform-admin is in role-platform-admin only, which maps to the existing owner Polaris role and an identical RustFS policy instead of a new Polaris role.
The two repositories are independent: only Airflow's Git clone of Bundles links them.
implementation_decisions: New confidential client lakehouse-writer: password grant only, 3600 s tokens, Polaris role mapper; the writer password file is written from the JSON by prepare-lakehouse-runtime.py.
The Bundle validator checks the host root only with --host-paths (host); the copy inside the image checks only the Bundle configuration.
grant_realm_admin gives role-platform-admin the realm-management realm-admin role of the lakehouse realm; JupyterHub allowed_groups and admin_groups include role-platform-admin.
deviations: Build and Test found an airflow-init failure caused by removing LAKEHOUSE_PROJECT_ROOT; fixed with the --host-paths flag and two tests.
Keycloak realm-admin and JupyterHub admin for role-platform-admin were added during Build and Test at the user's request (FR-4 change notes).
A Jenkins home backup was taken before the reset; the reset removed the Jenkins CI job, which was not restored.
superseded_decisions: write-service-account (client credentials) replaced by srv-default-writer through lakehouse-writer (password grant).
The platform-admin user with a generated one-time password in the owner group replaced by platform-admin with ChangeM3! in role-platform-admin; .runtime/credentials/platform-admin-password retired.
Airflow Bundles at ../opensource-lakehouse/.runtime/airflow-dag-bundles with LAKEHOUSE_PROJECT_ROOT replaced by <infra-v2>/.runtime/airflow-dag-bundles; knowledge/opensource-lakehouse retired.
The Jenkins home as a verified copy of the legacy home replaced by a fresh home after the reset (backup kept).
follow_ups: Restore the Jenkins CI job from .runtime/backups/20261031-pre-reset/jenkins-home.tar.gz, or define it as code.
Unexplained disappearance of stopped hive-dremio-rustfs-* and iceberg-poc-* containers during Build and Test (volumes intact; not the reset).

# Application Design — Keycloak, Polaris, RustFS, Jenkins, and Console/UI SSO

## Purpose

This project provides a local Docker Compose lakehouse platform-admin journey. It bootstraps an initial `default` lakehouse data product without migrating legacy Hive or FreeIPA state. The journey provisions:

- identity groups
- storage buckets
- Polaris catalogs and namespaces
- authorization grants
- RustFS console policies
- Spark smoke tables across production, dev, and UAT

## Components

- **Keycloak** provides the `lakehouse` OIDC realm, the four product role groups plus `role-platform-admin`, five bootstrap users, the `lakehouse-writer` workload client, and browser-login clients for JupyterHub, Airflow, the RustFS console, and Jenkins. See `functional-design/lakehouse-product-access.md`.
- **Apache Polaris** provides Iceberg REST and management APIs, catalogs, namespaces, principal roles, grants, and scoped RustFS credential vending.
- **PostgreSQL** stores Keycloak and Polaris state in separate databases and named volumes.
- **RustFS** (1.0.4) provides the three S3-compatible environment buckets. Bootstrap creates missing resources and preserves existing objects. Its console accepts Keycloak OIDC sign-in, with root static keys kept as break-glass.
- **Host scripts** prepare protected credentials, start/check/stop/reset local services, enforce the bootstrap users, and run idempotent data-product, RustFS policy, and Airflow bootstrap operations.
- **Apache Airflow** provides the production/UAT workload control plane and browser UI. It uses FAB authentication through Keycloak, with a local administrator recovery login.
- **Spark** runs on-demand Iceberg workloads using workload-specific OAuth identities and Polaris-vended S3 credentials.
- **JupyterHub** remains a separately supported interactive service with user-bound Spark authentication.
- **Jenkins** (2.580.1) runs the CI for the `opensource-lakehouse` workload repository. It was migrated from the pre-v2 instance and uses Keycloak SSO. See `functional-design/jenkins-ci-access.md`.
- **Deferred and retired**: StarRocks remains deferred. FreeIPA, Hive Metastore, and MIT Kerberos are retired from the target default runtime, as are the FreeIPA-era RustFS identity scripts.

## Repository independence

This repository runs on its own. The only link to the `opensource-lakehouse` workload repository is Airflow cloning its Git Bundles over HTTPS into this repository's `.runtime/airflow-dag-bundles`. No sibling checkout is mounted or referenced, and there is no `LAKEHOUSE_PROJECT_ROOT` setting. The workload repository supplies DAGs, configuration, notebooks, and workload entry points. Its own knowledge documents were retired on 2026-10-31.

## Airflow and shared Spark runtime

The Airflow control plane and writer token broker run in the v2 Compose boundary. For each DAG run, Airflow:
1. resolves the selected Git Bundle revision
2. registers run-scoped broker state
3. creates an ephemeral Spark container with the bundle mounted read-only

The writer identity is the Keycloak user `srv-default-writer` (group `role-default-writer`). The broker gets its tokens through the password grant on the confidential `lakehouse-writer` client. The client secret and the user's password (`.runtime/credentials/srv-default-writer-password`, written from `infra/keycloak/bootstrap-users.json`) stay in the broker and Spark-bootstrap boundary. Polaris sees the principal `srv-default-writer`. Spark receives an initial access token and a run-scoped renewal capability, never the secret or password.

Per-run execution contract:
1. Airflow resolves a run against the pinned checkout of the production or UAT Bundle.
2. The broker gets a writer token, associates it with that DAG run, and issues a high-entropy, run-scoped renewal capability.
3. Airflow starts one ephemeral Spark container, mounts the Bundle read-only, and passes only the initial token, broker endpoint and CA, run handle, and capability.
4. The Iceberg `AuthManager` renews the token through the broker over authenticated TLS. Polaris enforces the writer role and vends scoped RustFS credentials.
5. On completion or failure, Airflow removes the container and revokes broker run state. Run state also expires on its own.

Broker registration or renewal failures fail the task; there is no fallback identity.

The shared runtime uses Spark 3.5.5, Java 17, and Iceberg 1.10.2. Its JVM `AuthManager` renews access tokens through identity-specific adapters: Airflow uses the run-scoped writer broker, and Jupyter Spark uses the authenticated user's Hub broker. These identities and capabilities are not interchangeable. Polaris remains the authorization and scoped RustFS credential vending point; no RustFS root credential is handed to Spark.

The Airflow contract preserves two Git Bundles: `lakehouse-main` tracking `main` and `lakehouse-uat` tracking `uat`. `infra/airflow/validate-bundle-config.py` checks this list. With `--host-paths`, which `scripts/lakehouse.sh` passes, it also checks that the host Bundle root is this repository's `.runtime/airflow-dag-bundles`. The copy inside the image checks only the Bundle configuration. The writer client has a one-hour access-token lifetime override; human JupyterHub token lifetimes remain unchanged.

## Airflow browser authentication

The Airflow API server uses FAB OIDC with the confidential `airflow` client in the Keycloak `lakehouse` realm.

- **Endpoints**: browser authorization uses the host-reachable Keycloak hostname; token and user-info requests use Docker networking.
- **Token validation**: the configured issuer is validated explicitly. The RS256 JWKS is fetched from the internal Keycloak service address, so Docker loopback resolution does not send the request back to Airflow.
- **Callbacks**: the exact local callback URLs are `http://localhost:8085/auth/oauth-authorized/keycloak` and `http://127.0.0.1:8085/auth/oauth-authorized/keycloak`.
- **Exposure and recovery**: the Airflow service stays loopback-bound. The local FAB password login is a separate recovery route restricted to `AIRFLOW_ADMIN_USERNAME`.

| Keycloak group | Airflow role (as approved by the Airflow SSO intent) |
|---|---|
| `role-default-owner` | `Admin` |
| `role-default-developer` | `Admin` |
| `role-default-analyst` | `User` |
| `role-default-writer` | `Viewer` |
| `role-platform-admin` | `Admin` |

Users without an approved group are denied OAuth login. The Airflow OIDC integration is browser-only and does not change API or service-account authentication.

> As of 2026-10-30, `infra/airflow/airflow_sso_roles.py` and `webserver_config.py` map `role-default-developer` to `User`. This change was made outside any AI-DLC intent; `tests/airflow/test_keycloak_sso_contract.py` still expects `Admin`. Reconcile this table, the code, and the tests in a dedicated change.

## RustFS console authentication

**Login flow**
- The RustFS console offers Keycloak sign-in through the confidential `rustfs` client in the `lakehouse` realm: Authorization Code with PKCE S256.
- The callback is derived from the browser host: `http://{localhost,127.0.0.1}:<console port>/rustfs/admin/v3/oidc/callback/default`. The console port is `RUSTFS_CONSOLE_HOST_PORT`, default 9001.
- Keycloak registers exactly those two callbacks, plus the post-logout URIs `.../rustfs/console/auth/login`. RustFS rejects static loopback redirect URIs, so the exact Keycloak list is the allowlist. Logins started on the S3 port fail at Keycloak.

**Reaching Keycloak**
- Keycloak advertises `keycloak.localhost:8080` for token, JWKS, and logout endpoints, and that name resolves to loopback inside containers.
- RustFS therefore reaches Keycloak over the internal network `lakehouse-local_rustfs-identity`, where Keycloak carries the alias `keycloak.localhost`. No other service joins that network.
- `RUSTFS_OUTBOUND_ALLOW_ORIGINS` allows exactly `http://keycloak.localhost:8080`.
- The `lakehouse-rustfs-groups` mapper puts `groups` in the ID token.

**Client secret**
- The secret is `.runtime/credentials/rustfs-oidc-client-secret`.
- `infra/rustfs/rustfs-entrypoint.sh` exports it into the RustFS process at start, because RustFS 1.0.4 has no file-based OIDC secret setting.
- It is absent from Compose files and `docker inspect`.

**Authorization and sessions**
- RustFS uses each `groups` value as a policy name. The four product-group policies are described in `functional-design/lakehouse-product-access.md`.
- Users with no matching policy are refused a session. Console sessions last one hour.
- Logout is RP-initiated through Keycloak.
- If Keycloak is unavailable, new OIDC logins fail, existing sessions run to expiry, and RustFS retries discovery.

**Root and Polaris**: root static keys remain the break-glass console login and the identity Polaris uses server-side for STS.

**Known upstream limitation**: RustFS 1.0.4 embeds console v0.1.37. Its bucket-list page (`/rustfs/console/browser/`) remounts in a loop for non-admin users, which includes every OIDC user ([rustfs/console#271](https://github.com/rustfs/console/issues/271); fixed in console v0.1.38). Users open a bucket directly at `/rustfs/console/browser?bucket=<name>`. Follow-up: adopt the first RustFS release that bundles console v0.1.38 or later, and re-check the console's metadata-action needs.

## Jenkins CI authentication

**Service**
- Jenkins runs as the core Compose service `jenkins` on `127.0.0.1:${JENKINS_HOST_PORT:-8090}`.
- Its home is `lakehouse-local_jenkins-home`. It was first a verified copy of the legacy `iceberg-poc-jenkins-home`, and the legacy container and volume were removed on 2026-10-31.
- The environment reset on 2026-10-31 deleted that home. Jenkins now starts with a `fresh` marker and no workload job. The pre-reset home is saved at `.runtime/backups/20261031-pre-reset/jenkins-home.tar.gz`. Restoring the `opensource-lakehouse-dp/opensource-lakehouse-ci` job, or defining it as code, is open.

**Plugins**
- The image pins exactly 104 plugins in `infra/jenkins/plugins.txt`: the legacy versions plus `oic-auth 4.731.v4932b_506e767` and `nimbus-jose-jwt-api`.
- The build fails on any mismatch, and `PLUGINS_FORCE_UPGRADE=true` makes the image authoritative over the home's plugins.

**Configuration as code**
- `infra/jenkins/casc/jenkins.yaml` holds the OIDC realm, the authorization matrix, the escape hatch, executors, mode, crumb issuer, and root URL. It is reapplied at every start.
- Endpoints follow the Airflow pattern: browser redirects use `keycloak.localhost:8080`; token, JWKS, and userinfo calls use `keycloak:8080`; the issuer is the canonical one. No network alias is needed.

**Keycloak client and secrets**
- The confidential `jenkins` client uses PKCE S256, exact `finishLogin` callbacks and `/` post-logout URIs for both loopback hosts, and a `groups` claim in the ID token (`lakehouse-jenkins-groups`).
- The client secret and the escape-hatch password are protected files read through `${trim:${readFile:...}}`.

**Builds**: pipelines run on the built-in node without the Docker socket. GitHub is scanned anonymously.

## Resource and data role model

| Environment | Catalog | Namespace | Bucket |
|---|---|---|---|
| Production | `lakehouse` | `default_lh` | `bucket-default` |
| UAT | `lakehouse_uat` | `default_lhuat` | `bucket-default-uat` |
| Dev | `lakehouse_dev` | `default_lhdev` | `bucket-default-dev` |

Each catalog's default base location is `<bucket>/<catalog>/`, and its database namespace contributes the next path segment. Iceberg tables therefore resolve beneath `<bucket>/<catalog>/<database>/<table>` exactly once. For example, the production smoke table is `s3://bucket-default/lakehouse/default_lh/bootstrap_smoke_test/`.

Role semantics, Polaris grants, and RustFS console policies are described in `functional-design/lakehouse-product-access.md`. Polaris enforces catalog operations. Polaris-vended credentials constrain object access for workloads, and the group-named RustFS policies constrain direct console access. These data-platform privileges are distinct from the Airflow UI role mapping above.

## Startup and bootstrap

**Core start.** The local runtime starts Keycloak, its PostgreSQL database, Polaris, its PostgreSQL database, and RustFS. `scripts/lakehouse.sh start`:
1. creates only missing protected runtime credentials, including the RustFS OIDC client secret
2. runs the required Polaris schema initialization
3. waits for health
4. runs the Keycloak realm bootstrap. It creates the five groups, the clients (including `rustfs`, `jenkins`, and `lakehouse-writer`), and any missing bootstrap users. It gives `role-platform-admin` the `lakehouse` realm's `realm-admin` role, and never changes an existing user
5. starts JupyterHub
6. builds the pinned Jenkins image, runs `scripts/migrate-jenkins-home.py` (copy once, verify, mark; refuse to overwrite; empty home with a notice when no legacy home exists), and starts Jenkins

**Product bootstrap.** `scripts/bootstrap-default-product.sh` provisions provider resources and grants:
1. reruns `start` and the realm bootstrap, then `scripts/bootstrap-users.sh`, which resets the five bootstrap users to their default password and single group
2. creates the buckets, then the five RustFS group policies
3. creates catalogs and grants, and reconciles memberships
4. verifies writer authentication
5. runs Spark smoke-table create/write/read checks

Reruns preserve bucket objects and do not duplicate smoke rows. The realm and policy bootstraps refuse conflicting existing configuration. The only automatic change to existing configuration is narrow: a policy that exactly equals its previous approved definition is upgraded. `scripts/verify-rustfs-oidc.py` and `scripts/verify-jenkins-oidc.py` check the RustFS and Jenkins OIDC wiring read-only. `scripts/lakehouse.sh stop` stops Jenkins too and preserves named volumes. The guarded `scripts/lakehouse.sh remove-legacy-jenkins --confirm` removes only the pre-v2 Jenkins container and volume, and only once the v2 home is a verified copy and healthy.

**Reset.** `scripts/lakehouse.sh reset` (`scripts/reset-lakehouse.py`) deletes all local platform state:
- `lakehouse-local` containers, plus Jupyter user servers and Airflow Spark runs by runtime-role label
- the six data volumes and the `lakehouse-jupyter-home-*` volumes
- the six networks
- `.runtime/credentials`, `.runtime/container-mounts`, and `.runtime/airflow-dag-bundles`

It lists what it will delete first. It needs the typed word `reset`, or `--yes`, and `--dry-run` only lists. A path guard refuses symlinks and other paths. Images, other projects, other `.runtime` entries such as `backups`, and anything outside the repository are kept. It is irreversible, and a rebuild is `bootstrap-default-product.sh`.

**Airflow.** `scripts/lakehouse.sh start-airflow`:
1. prepares Airflow secrets and certificates
2. additively bootstraps the Keycloak Airflow client and group mapper
3. builds the Airflow images
4. starts the Airflow control plane and dependencies
5. waits for service readiness
6. verifies production/UAT DAG registration without running DAGs

`scripts/lakehouse.sh stop-airflow` stops Airflow services and Spark runs while preserving provider data, Airflow metadata, and Bundle checkouts. Keycloak clients and mappers are persistent realm configuration and are not removed by stopping services.

**Secrets.** All published host endpoints bind to loopback. Protected credentials remain under `.runtime/credentials/` and must be backed up separately using encrypted storage. No secrets belong in source control, reports, or command output.

## Verification status and known limits

**Platform bootstrap.** U1 runtime readiness, U2 writer and negative-token checks, U3 RustFS bucket/STS checks, and the U4 end-to-end bootstrap and four-role positive/negative Spark access matrix passed on the local `linux/arm64` Docker engine. During a Keycloak outage, new token issuance and group reconciliation fail, while already-issued unexpired access tokens may continue until expiry.

**Airflow writer token.** For this intent:
- builds, static checks, and automated suites passed
- the designated main E2E run passed
- the user subsequently reported building the shared image and successful main and UAT DAG runs

Those later run IDs and revisions were not independently retrievable in that session and are recorded as user-confirmed.

**Airflow Keycloak SSO.** Verification:
- the client contract tests (8) and SSO authorization tests (6) passed after the runtime corrections
- the local Airflow API/UI returned HTTP 200
- both exact callbacks matched
- the running FAB client retrieved the RS256 JWKS
- production/UAT DAG registrations were verified without running a DAG

Successful interactive login and role assignment after the JWKS correction were not verified. The user accepted that verification limitation as a waiver; it is not a successful end-to-end authentication result.

**RustFS console OIDC** (2026-10-30), verification passed:
- the RustFS, Keycloak, and Polaris suites (84 tests, including Hypothesis policy properties)
- `verify-rustfs-oidc.py` (7/7)
- bootstrap idempotency
- the Polaris STS regression check
- a headless login and authorization run with temporary users (19/19: per-role access, refusal without a product group, RP-initiated logout)
- a user-confirmed interactive developer login through a bucket view

The upstream bucket-list loop above is a documented limitation.

**Jenkins onboarding and SSO** (2026-10-31). Passed:
- `verify-jenkins-oidc.py` 9/9, also after a restart
- idempotent bootstrap and migration reruns
- the plugin set equals `plugins.txt`
- a verified home copy
- a headless SSO and permission run with temporary users: owner Administer; developer read and build; analyst read-only; writer and no-group users denied; escape hatch; logout
- RustFS, Airflow, and JupyterHub unaffected
- an interactive login confirmed by the user

**Verification waiver (user-accepted; not a pass)**: no successful workload CI build. `main` #11 and `uat` #4 ran the full pipeline and failed on one `opensource-lakehouse` unit test after commit `00b6623` ("rename dag"), a workload regression outside scope.

**Environment reset and bootstrap users** (2026-10-31). Passed:
- a real reset and a rebuild from nothing
- all five users log in with the default password, with one group each and the right Polaris role
- rerunning `bootstrap-users.sh` restored the defaults after deliberate changes, and left other users alone
- RustFS OIDC and STS, the Polaris negative cases, and the role matrix
- an Airflow broker token as `srv-default-writer`
- platform-admin realm administration: 200 on `lakehouse`, 403 on `master`
- a user-confirmed JupyterHub login

The Jenkins verifier passed 8 of 9; the CI job is absent after the reset. Not run: the Keycloak outage test.

**Not run anywhere**: performance and vulnerability scanning.

**Other known limits.**
- The prior bootstrap intent's closure was user-approved with a verification waiver. For that intent, the human PKCE callback browser flow and some reconciliation failure-path diagnostics were not tested.
- The reconciler and the realm bootstrap use a protected Keycloak bootstrap administrator. Replace it with a least-privilege identity before shared deployment.
- The approved Polaris `require-header=false` setting was specific to the single configured realm and earlier Iceberg 1.8.1 behavior. Reassess strict realm-header enforcement before adding realms.
- Concurrent workload, resilience, and live role-matrix checks remain unverified where noted in their respective intent records.
- This local single-node setup is not a production, HA, or multi-host certification.

## Operational entry points

See `README.md` for starting and resetting the platform (two-step start, bootstrap users, reset scope), operator commands, RustFS console OIDC login (including break-glass, secret rotation, and the bucket-link workaround), Jenkins CI and Keycloak SSO (permissions, break-glass, migration, legacy removal), the guarded one-time local storage reset, backup guidance, and shutdown boundaries. Detailed intent designs and test reports are preserved in the intent archives, most recently [Environment Reset and Bootstrap Users](../../archive/20261031-environment-reset-bootstrap-users/intent-summary.md), [Jenkins Onboarding and Keycloak SSO](../../archive/20261031-jenkins-keycloak-sso/intent-summary.md), [RustFS Keycloak OIDC](../../archive/20261030-rustfs-keycloak-oidc/intent-summary.md), and [Airflow Keycloak SSO](../../archive/20261029-airflow-keycloak-sso/intent-summary.md).

# Functional Design — Lakehouse Product Access

Current functional design of the `default` data product's access model across Keycloak, Polaris, and RustFS. This file was relocated on 2026-10-30 from the retired `knowledge/hive-dremio-rustfs/functional-design/lakehouse-workload-and-access.md`, which is preserved in the [RustFS Keycloak OIDC intent archive](../../../archive/20261030-rustfs-keycloak-oidc/intent-summary.md). For architecture, see [`../application-design.md`](../application-design.md).

## Product roles

| Keycloak group / Polaris role | Production (`lakehouse`, `bucket-default`) | UAT (`lakehouse_uat`, `bucket-default-uat`) | Dev (`lakehouse_dev`, `bucket-default-dev`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `role-default-owner` | manage | manage | manage |
| `role-default-developer` | read | read | read/write |
| `role-default-analyst` | read | — | — |
| `role-default-writer` (service role) | read/write | read/write | read/write |
| `role-platform-admin` | manage (as owner) | manage (as owner) | manage (as owner) |

- **Owner** manages the product's Polaris resources and data across environments.
- **Writer**: the service user `srv-default-writer` reads and writes all environments.
- **Platform admin**: `role-platform-admin` is owner-equivalent and has no Polaris role of its own.
  - Its Keycloak group carries the Polaris client role `role-default-owner`, and the reconciler gives its members the `role-default-owner` principal role.
  - RustFS has a policy named `role-platform-admin` that is identical to the owner policy.

## Platform admin in each service

| Service | `role-platform-admin` | `role-default-owner` |
|---|---|---|
| Polaris and RustFS | owner rights | owner rights |
| Airflow | `Admin` | `Admin` |
| Jenkins | `Overall/Administer` | `Overall/Administer` |
| JupyterHub | admitted, and Hub admin | not admitted |
| Keycloak | `realm-admin` of the `lakehouse` realm (`realm-management` client); no `master` access | none |

JupyterHub admits `role-default-developer`, `role-default-analyst`, and `role-platform-admin`. The Keycloak and JupyterHub rights were added at the user's request during the reset intent's Build and Test.

## Bootstrap identities (`infra/keycloak/bootstrap-users.json`)

| User | Group |
|---|---|
| `joe-developer` | `role-default-developer` |
| `peter-analyst` | `role-default-analyst` |
| `maria-owner` | `role-default-owner` |
| `srv-default-writer` | `role-default-writer` |
| `platform-admin` | `role-platform-admin` |

- **Password**: every user gets the documented local-development password `ChangeM3!`. It is permanent, with no required actions, and the email is `<user>@lakehouse.local`.
- **Create-only at start**: `infra/keycloak/bootstrap-realm.py` creates only missing users and never changes an existing user.
- **Enforce on demand**: `scripts/bootstrap-users.sh` (`infra/keycloak/bootstrap-users.py`) changes only the listed users. For each one it:
  - creates the user or updates the profile
  - resets the password, non-temporary
  - clears required actions
  - removes every other group
  - adds the default group

  It fails if the realm groups are missing. `scripts/bootstrap-default-product.sh` runs it after the realm bootstrap. Reconcile Polaris afterwards.
- **Writer credential**: `scripts/prepare-lakehouse-runtime.py` writes the writer's password file from the same JSON. A changed `srv-default-writer` password breaks Airflow and Spark writes until `bootstrap-users.sh` restores it.
- **Writer client**: `lakehouse-writer` is confidential, password grant only, with no browser flow and no service account. Tokens last 3600 s and carry the Polaris role mapper. It accepts any realm user's credentials, but tokens carry only that user's roles.

## Authorization layers
1. **Identity**: Keycloak groups supply identity and role claims.
2. **Catalog**: Polaris maps the approved role claims to Polaris principal roles and catalog grants. Polaris-mediated Iceberg access vends scoped, short-lived RustFS credentials. Workloads (Spark through Airflow or JupyterHub) never receive root or static RustFS credentials.
3. **Console**: RustFS console sessions carry the policies named by the user's `groups` claim. They govern direct object access in the console only.

These layers are independent:
- Keycloak membership alone creates no Polaris grant; principals must be reconciled (`infra/polaris/reconcile-keycloak-groups.py`).
- Polaris grants do not grant RustFS console access.
- RustFS console policies do not grant catalog operations.

## RustFS console policies (`infra/rustfs/bootstrap-policies.py`)

**Policy shape**
- Each product group, and `role-platform-admin`, has a RustFS IAM policy of exactly the same name.
- Every policy allows `s3:ListAllMyBuckets` on `arn:aws:s3:::*`, which reveals bucket names only.
- Every other resource is one of the three bucket ARNs or their `/*` object ARNs.
- Statements are allow-only, and no policy contains an `admin:` action.

**Access levels**

| Level | Bucket actions | Object actions |
|---|---|---|
| read | `GetBucketLocation`, `ListBucket`, plus console metadata reads: `GetBucketPolicyStatus`, `GetBucketVersioning`, `GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration`, `GetBucketTagging`, `ListBucketVersions` | `GetObject`, `GetObjectTagging`, `GetObjectVersion`, `GetObjectRetention`, `GetObjectLegalHold` |
| read/write | read + `ListBucketMultipartUploads` | read + `PutObject`, `DeleteObject`, `AbortMultipartUpload`, `ListMultipartUploadParts` |
| manage | `s3:*` on the bucket and its objects | |

**Rules**
- A user in several groups receives the union of their policies; effective access per bucket is the highest level among the user's groups.
- A user with no group value naming an existing policy is refused a console session by RustFS. Other group values are ignored.
- **Bootstrap**:
  - creates missing policies
  - accepts canonically equal ones (order-insensitive comparison)
  - upgrades a policy only if it exactly equals its previous approved definition, the one without console metadata reads
  - refuses any other existing content without changing it, naming only the policy

## Failure behavior
- **Keycloak unavailable**: new token issuance, group reconciliation, and new RustFS OIDC logins fail. Already-issued tokens and console sessions remain usable until expiry. Root break-glass access to RustFS is unaffected.
- **Polaris principals**: Polaris needs a principal record for each Keycloak username before that user's data queries can be authorized. Reconcile after creating users or changing memberships.
- **Reconciler identity**: the reconciler and realm bootstrap currently use the protected local Keycloak bootstrap administrator. Replace it with a least-privilege identity before shared deployment.

## Verification
- **Environment reset (2026-10-31)**:
  - a rebuild from nothing; five bootstrap logins with one group each and the right Polaris role
  - `bootstrap-users.sh` restored the defaults after password, group, and required-action changes, and left a user outside the list alone
  - platform-admin got 200 on the `lakehouse` admin API and 403 on `master`; owner got 403
  - JupyterHub login confirmed by the user
- **Spark journey (U4)**: the Spark smoke-table journey and positive/negative read/write behavior verified for developer, analyst, owner, and writer in all environments.
- **Token handling (U2)**: wrong-audience and expired-token rejection, and Keycloak-outage behavior, verified. That intent closed under a waiver for the human PKCE callback and some reconciliation failure paths.
- **RustFS console (2026-10-30)**:
  - property-based tests over the policy definitions
  - a headless login and authorization run with temporary users: analyst read-only on production and denied elsewhere; developer writes dev only; console metadata reads allowed in scope and denied out of scope; refusal without a product group
  - a user-confirmed interactive developer login through a bucket view
- **Known limitation**: the RustFS 1.0.4 console bucket-list page loops for non-admin users (rustfs/console#271). Use `/rustfs/console/browser?bucket=<name>`.

# Functional Design — Jenkins CI and Access

Current functional design of the v2 Jenkins component. For architecture, see [`../application-design.md`](../application-design.md). History is in the [Jenkins Onboarding and Keycloak SSO intent archive](../../../archive/20261031-jenkins-keycloak-sso/intent-summary.md).

## Responsibility
Jenkins runs the CI for the `opensource-lakehouse` workload repository through the multibranch pipeline `opensource-lakehouse-dp/opensource-lakehouse-ci`. It scans `https://github.com/cdiogo1979/opensource-lakehouse/` anonymously on its schedule and runs that repository's `Jenkinsfile` (venv, compile, lint, flake8, bandit, pytest) on the built-in node with 2 executors. It has no Docker socket and no webhooks. There is no job for this infrastructure repository.

## Access rules
| Keycloak group / identity | Jenkins permissions |
|---|---|
| `role-default-owner` | `Overall/Administer` |
| `role-platform-admin` | `Overall/Administer` |
| `jenkins-break-glass` (escape hatch) | `Overall/Administer` |
| `role-default-developer` | `Overall/Read`, `Job/Read`, `Job/Build`, `Job/Cancel`, `Job/Workspace` |
| `role-default-analyst` | `Overall/Read`, `Job/Read` |
| `role-default-writer`, users without a group, anonymous | none |

- **Authorities**: group names arrive as plain values of the ID-token `groups` claim. A user in several groups receives the union of their permissions.
- **Sign-in**: people sign in through the Keycloak `jenkins` client only. The legacy local user database remains in the home but is not a login path.
- **Escape hatch**: the `jenkins-break-glass` login uses a protected password file. The plugin stores it BCrypt-hashed. It keeps working when Keycloak is unavailable.

## Configuration authority
- **Plugins**: `infra/jenkins/plugins.txt` (104 exact versions) is the plugin source of truth. The image overrides the home's plugins at start, and there are no runtime installs.
- **Security as code**: `infra/jenkins/casc/jenkins.yaml` owns the security realm, authorization matrix, escape hatch, executors, mode, crumb issuer, and root URL. It is reapplied at every start, so UI changes to these are overwritten. Jobs and build history are migrated state, not code.
- **Secrets**: the client secret and the break-glass password come from mounted files. Nothing secret is written to configuration as code, Compose, or the container environment.

## Home lifecycle (`scripts/migrate-jenkins-home.py`)
| Observed state | Action |
|---|---|
| Origin marker present | Skip |
| Non-empty without marker | Refuse; start-up stops for review |
| Empty, legacy volume present, legacy container running | Refuse |
| Empty, legacy volume present, legacy stopped | Copy (source read-only), verify file count and content digest, write `migrated:<volume> <time>` marker last |
| Empty, no legacy volume | Write a `fresh` marker; start empty with a notice that the job must be restored or recreated |

The legacy instance was removed on 2026-10-31 with the guarded `remove-legacy-jenkins --confirm`. That command requires a `migrated:` marker, a healthy v2 Jenkins, and a stopped legacy container, and it removes only the named legacy container and volume.

## Failure behavior
- **Keycloak unavailable**: SSO logins fail, the escape hatch works, and builds continue.
- **Copy verification failure**: the target is not marked, and the next start refuses until the operator reviews and removes the partial volume.
- **Plugin mismatch at image build**: the build fails.

## Verification and known limits
- Verified 2026-10-31:
  - the permission matrix for every group, plus refusal of users without a group
  - escape hatch and logout
  - plugin parity and the migration
  - restart and idempotency
  - an interactive login
- **Waived**: a successful workload CI build. The `opensource-lakehouse` commit `00b6623` broke one unit test, so `main` #11 and `uat` #4 fail at pytest after all other stages pass.
- Pipelines needing Docker are not supported.
- **Reset (2026-10-31)**: `scripts/lakehouse.sh reset` deletes `lakehouse-local_jenkins-home`, including jobs and build history, because jobs are not configuration as code.
  - After the reset, Jenkins started with a `fresh` marker and no workload job.
  - The pre-reset home is saved at `.runtime/backups/20261031-pre-reset/jenkins-home.tar.gz` (SHA-256 alongside).
  - Open: restore the job, or define it as code, for example with Job DSL in CasC.
- Back up `lakehouse-local_jenkins-home` before any reset.
